Comparing data is very useful when decisions need to be made in a ladder logic program. This data could be from inputs, timers, counters, or any other data-generating source.

LESSON MENU
COMPARISON INSTRUCTIONS
In ladder logic programming, you may need to make comparisons of data items within the data files. There are many different types of comparison instructions.
DISCUSSION
The list below shows the comparison instructions used by many PLCs. We will examine each of these instructions to see how they compare data and what type of output they provide.

This is the Equal (EQ) instruction. This instruction takes two parameters, source A and source B. Both A and B are word values. Remember, a word is 16 bits long. If any two bits in A and B don't match, they are not equal...

Source A is a word address in a data file. In other words, you specify the location of a word in memory that you want to use for a comparison. Source B can be either a word address in memory or the actual value you want to use...

The advantage of using word addresses in memory is that you can change the comparison value if you want. If you enter the comparison value directly, you will not be able to change it in your ladder logic evaluation...

The EQU instruction, like all comparison instructions, is entered into the left side of a ladder logic program rung. These instructions affect the logic path used by operation instructions on the right side of a rung...
If the two word values are not equal, the logic path through the instruction remains false. If they are equal, there will be a true logic path through the instruction..
The next instruction we are going to look at is the Not Equal (NEQ) instruction. This instruction requires the same parameters as the EQU instruction, source A and source B.
NOT EQUAL
This instruction works exactly opposite of the EQU instruction. If source A and source B do not equal each other, a true logic path exists. If they are equal, the logic path remains false.
This is the Less Than (LES) instruction. Again, this
comparison instruction requires the same parameters,
source A and source B. The instruction provides a true logic path if the value in A is less than the value in B...
LESS THAN
If the value in A is equal to or greater than B, the logic path will be false. It is important to note that this instruction has a range of true results and a range of false results.

The next instruction is the Less Than or Equal (LEQ) instruction. This instruction is a combination of the EQU and LES instructions shown below. If A is less than or equal to B, a true logic path exists...

The Greater Than (GRT) instruction decides if the value of A is greater than the value of B. If A is greater, a true logic path will exist. If the value is less than or equal to the value of B, the logic path is false...
GREATER THAN
This instruction is the Greater Than or Equal (GEQ) instruction. Just like the LEQ instruction, this instruction is a combination of EQU and GRT. The diagram below shows this combination.
If the value in A is greater than or equal to the value in B, a true logic path will exist. If the value is less than B, the logic path is false.
This instruction is the Masked Comparison for Equal (MEQ) instruction. It works similar to the EQU instruction, except for the fact that certain bits can be "masked" out.
MASKED EQUAL
EXAMPLE OF MASKING
Remember, This Instruction Actually uses 16 BIT Values, not 4.

In more general terms, masking is a process for comparing only certain bits. This instruction requires three parameters: a source, a mask, and a compare. The source is the word you would like to compare...

The mask contains a hexadecimal value that represents the bits you would like to test. Any ones in the mask will be tested; any zeros will not. This mask works in the same manner as the ones described in the lesson on I/O instructions...

The compare parameter is the word location or actual data that you want to compare to the source. If the source bits that have a one in the mask are the same as those bits in the compare, a true logic path is allowed...
If any of the bits that have a one in the mask are not the same, the logic path will be false. The diagram below illustrates the usage of a mask and an example of its results.

The last instruction that we are going to look at is the Limit Test (LIM) instruction. This instruction looks to see if a data value is within or outside a certain range, depending on how you use the instruction...
LIMIT TEST

This instruction requires three parameters: Low Limit, Test, and High Limit. The low and high limits set the range for the test. The test parameter is the value you are evaluating to see if it's within a specific range..

Both the low limit and high limit can have word addresses or actual values in them. Remember, if you use word addresses, you can change the values at those word locations in your ladder logic code while it is being evaluated...
If the low limit value is less than the high limit value, the instruction tests to see if the test value is within a range. If that value is within the range, a true logic path exists.
The diagram below shows which value will make a true logic path and which will make a false one for a hypothetical limit test case.
If the low limit value is higher than the high limit value, the instruction tests to see if the test data is outside of the specified range. Again, the diagram below shows an example of this case.
We have examined the different types of comparison instructions. Using them together can provide an endless number of comparison possibilities.

1. The Equal (EQU) instruction is used to test if two data values are equal. If both values are equal, a true logic path results; otherwise, the logic path is false.
2. The Not Equal (NEQ) instruction is used to test if two data values are not equal. If the values are not equal, a true logic path results; otherwise, the logic path is false.
NOT EQUAL

3. The Less Than (LES) instruction is used to test if a data value is less than another data value. If the first specified data value is less than the second data value, a true logic path results; otherwise, the logic path is false.
LESS THAN

4. The Less Than or Equal (LEQ) instruction is used to test if a data value is less than or equal to another data value. If the first specified data value is less than or equal to the second data value, a true logic path exists; otherwise, the logic path is false.

5. The Greater Than (GRT) instruction is used to test if a data value is greater than another data value. If the first specified data value is greater than the second value, a true logic path exists; otherwise, the logic path is false.
GREATER THAN

6. The Greater Than or Equal (GEQ) instruction is used to test if a data value is greater than or equal to another data value. If the first specified data value is greater than or equal to the second value, a true logic path exists; otherwise the logic path is false.

7. The Masked Comparison for Equal (MEQ) instruction is used to test if specific bits of a data value are equal to those bits of another data value. sk is used to determine which bits are to be compared; one is to compare and zero is to ignore. If all bits of the first data value with one in the mask are equal to the second data value, a true logic path exists; otherwise, the logic path is false.
MASKED EQUAL

A mask is used to determine which bits are to be compared; one is to compare and zero is to ignore. If all bits of the first data value with one in the mask are equal to the second data value, a true logic path exists; otherwise, the logic path is false.....................................

8. The Limit Test (LIM) instruction is used to see if a data value is within a specified range based on the instruction parameters. If the low limit is higher than the high limit, you want to see if the value is outside the range.
LIMIT TEST

9. If the low limit is lower than the high limit, you want to see if the value is within the range. Depending on which comparison you are making, the logic path will be true if the value is within range.

The program shown below is the ladder logic program you are going to enter to demonstrate some of the comparison instructions that you learned in the first part of this lesson.
Before we actually enter the program into the PLC APS software, let's look at what the program should do. This will help us understand if the program is operating properly when we are testing it...

On the 5050-1 PC card, there are three switches that we will use for this program: two push button switches and a slide switch. In our program, we have two counters. We are using compare instructions to compare the counter values..
The START and STOP push buttons are used to increment or decrement the counter. The slide switch controls which counter the START and STOP buttons change.

The first rung of the ladder logic program checks to see if the START button, which is attached to input 0, is pushed in (high) and that the slide switch is in the on position. If the conditions are met, counter 0 is incremented with the CTU instruction...

Notice that the preset value is zero. We are not counting to a particular number, so the done bit has no meaning for us. For convenience, we have set the preset to zero to remind us we do not need the done bit..........

The next rung looks for the STOP button to be pushed in and the slide switch to be in the on, or right, position. If a true logic path can be traced through these instructions, counter 0 will be decremented by 1...

Rung 3 looks to see if the START button is pressed in and the slide switch is in the off, or left, position. If there is a true logic path through these bit instructions, counter 1 will be incremented by 1...

Rung 4 looks to see if the STOP button is pressed, and the slide switch is in the off position. If there is a true logic path through these bit instructions, counter 1 will be decremented by 1. s START and STOP increment, decrementing counter 1...

Remember, slide switch ON means START increments and STOP decrements counter 0. Slide switch OFF means START increments and STOP decrements counter 1.ctions, counter 1 will be decremented by 1. s START and STOP increment, decrementing counter 1...

In the next rung, we have the Less Than (LES) instruction. This instruction compares the accumulator of counter 0 and the accumulator of counter 1. Recall that the accumulator is the second word of a counter data file...

If the accumulator of counter 0 is less than counter 1, the next instruction, output enable, will turn on LED 0. The LED will only remain on while there is a true logic path through the LES instruction...
Rung 6 uses the Equal (EQU) instruction. Again, counter 0 accumulator and counter 1 accumulator are compared. While they are equal, LED 1 will be illuminated.

Finally, in the last rung, we are using the Greater Than (GRT) instruction. In this case, if the value in the counter 0 accumulator is greater than the value in the counter 1 accumulator, LED 2 will be illuminated...
When we modify the counter values using the switches of the 5050-1 card, we can observe the states of the LES, EQU, and GRT based on the input words to the instructions.
